video.title: Shoulder Adduction Unlocks the Tennis Forehand

classification.reason: The coach explains how shoulder adduction serves as the final link in the forehand kinetic chain, how to set up the contact zone, and how to probe the ball.

problem.title_as_question: How does shoulder adduction unlock the tennis forehand and contact consistency?
problem.definition: Shoulder adduction naturally pulls across the body and turns inward; if the contact zone is not oriented properly, the ball will be hit sideways, down, or framed. Players must understand this final link and position the body to harness it back-to-front.
problem.target_player: recreational players (2.5 to 4.5) who want clean, consistent contact without missing or framing

symptoms.description: Ball flies sideways and downward because the racket turns completely over during natural adduction.
Shanking or framing the ball off the outside edge of the frame when the ball is too far away.
String angle drastically over-rotates or closes by around 100 degrees through the contact zone instead of staying stable.

causes.statement: The natural movement of shoulder adduction pulls across the body rather than straight towards the target unless oriented properly.
Shoulder adduction naturally couples with internal shoulder rotation, which tends to turn the hand and racket face over.
The ball is outside the functional contact zone (too far or mistimed), leaving no available shoulder adduction range to hit forward.
The hitting elbow is stuck behind the plane of the hips, preventing effective shoulder adduction into the ball.
Allowing the string angle to completely close through contact rather than keeping it mostly consistent with only minor change.

angles.summary: Shoulder adduction is the final link in the kinetic chain; when the elbow passes the hip plane, cross-body pull translates into back-to-front forward drive.
Demonstrating how a naive adduction motion turns the racket completely over, sending the ball down and sideways.
Developing an internal sensation of passing through contact with a stable, slight downward string angle using shoulder adduction.
Body probing: tilting hips for low balls or adjusting spacing so that the ball meets the same optimal adduction zone relative to the torso.

solutions.summary: Pull across the body using shoulder adduction instead of pushing forward.
Check that the racket strings are on a slight downward angle at contact so the adduction motion drives the ball cleanly.
solutions.external_goal: Racket strings tilted on a slight downward angle through contact

solutions.summary: Make sure the elbow swings forward and passes the plane of the hips before initiating the final adduction link.
Figure out and probe where in front of you the ball must be positioned for shoulder adduction to drive forward.
solutions.external_goal: Position the ball in front where the adduction contact zone exists

solutions.summary: Tilt the hips and adjust torso posture to bring low balls into the exact same relative adduction contact spot.
solutions.external_goal: Match hip tilt to the ball height to keep the adduction window

solutions.summary: Shadow or slowly rehearse going through contact feeling a consistent string angle driven by shoulder adduction.
